options_en: The selection panel unanimously recommended the installation of a
highly efficient modern German steel surgical equipment in the
newly inaugurated trauma care unit of the government hospital.
No Error
options_hi: The selection panel unanimously recommended the installation of a
highly efficient modern German steel surgical equipment in the
newly inaugurated trauma care unit of the government hospital.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (D) - No Error.

Rule / Concept: OSASCOMP (Order of Adjectives)

When multiple adjectives are used before a noun, they must follow the fixed order:

Opinion → Size → Age → Shape → Color → Origin → Material → Purpose.

If this sequence is correctly maintained, the sentence is grammatically sound.

Application to the Given Question -

highly efficient → Opinion

modern → Age

German → Origin

Steel → Material

surgical → Purpose

The adjectives strictly follow the OSASCOMP order:

Opinion → Age → Origin → Material → Purpose,

hence no grammatical error exists in any part of the sentence.

More Examples for Clarity -

a beautiful Italian leather handbag.

an old Indian wooden temple door.

a modern German steel medical instrument.

Things to Remember / Exam Tips -

Always classify adjectives before judging correctness.

“No Error” options are often correct in well-balanced OSASCOMP sequences.

Ignore long modifiers and focus only on adjective order.

questions.q_en:
Select the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank.

Despite the unexpected technical glitch, she managed to __________ the live presentation with remarkable confidence.
questions.q_hi:
Select the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank.

Despite the unexpected technical glitch, she managed to __________ the live presentation with remarkable confidence.
options_en: carry out
carry on
carry off
carry away
options_hi: carry out
carry on
carry off
carry away
questions.solution_en:
Explanation: The correct answer is option (3).

English Explanation: “Carry off” means to succeed in doing something difficult or to handle a challenging situation confidently and successfully. In the sentence, despite the unexpected technical glitch, she handled the live presentation with confidence. Therefore, “carry off” correctly conveys the idea of managing a difficult situation successfully. “Carry out” means to execute or complete a task. “Carry on” means to continue something. “Carry away” means to lose control due to strong emotions. Since the context refers to handling a challenging situation successfully, “carry off” is the most appropriate fit.

1. Carry out (पूरा करना / कार्यान्वित करना)
Meaning in Hindi: किसी योजना या कार्य को लागू करना या पूरा करना।
Example: The team carried out the instructions carefully. (टीम ने निर्देशों को सावधानीपूर्वक पूरा किया।)

2. Carry on (जारी रखना)
Meaning in Hindi: किसी कार्य को जारी रखना।
Example: She carried on with her speech despite the noise. (शोर के बावजूद उसने अपना भाषण जारी रखा।)

3. Carry off (सफलतापूर्वक कर लेना / जीत लेना)
Meaning in Hindi: किसी कठिन कार्य को सफलतापूर्वक कर लेना या जीत लेना।
Example 1: It was a difficult speech, but he carried it off with great confidence. (यह एक कठिन भाषण था, लेकिन उसने इसे आत्मविश्वास के साथ सफलतापूर्वक पूरा किया।)
Example 2: She carried off the award for best researcher. (उसने सर्वश्रेष्ठ शोधकर्ता का पुरस्कार जीत लिया।)

4. Carry away (भावनाओं में बह जाना)
Meaning in Hindi: तीव्र भावनाओं के कारण नियंत्रण खो देना।
Example: He was carried away by excitement after the victory. (जीत के बाद वह उत्साह में बह गया।)

questions.q_en:
In the sentence below, identify the part of speech of the word “trained”:

Only highly trained officials were allowed to access the confidential records stored in the digital archive.
questions.q_hi:
In the sentence below, identify the part of speech of the word “trained”:

Only highly trained officials were allowed to access the confidential records stored in the digital archive.
options_en: Main Verb
Gerund
Participle/Adjective
Adverb
options_hi: Main Verb
Gerund
Participle/Adjective
Adverb
questions.solution_en:
Answer: C) Participle/Adjective

Explanation: A participle is a verb form that functions as an adjective. Past participles often end in -ed, -en, or irregular forms.

Here, “trained” describes the noun “officials.”

What kind of officials? → highly trained officials

Since it describes the noun rather than acting as the main verb, “trained” functions as a participle (adjectival participle).

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: To such an extent the multinational conglomerate has expanded
its operations into the emerging markets of Southeast Asia
that it now controls nearly forty percent of the regional market share.
No Error
options_hi: To such an extent the multinational conglomerate has expanded
its operations into the emerging markets of Southeast Asia
that it now controls nearly forty percent of the regional market share.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (A) Replace “the multinational conglomerate has” with “has the multinational conglomerate”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Inversion with "To such an extent/degree"

When a sentence begins with the phrase "To such an extent" or "To such a degree" to emphasize the intensity or scale of an action, the main clause must follow the Inversion structure. This means the auxiliary verb (has, have, was, were, did, etc.) must be placed before the subject. This structure is typically followed by a "that" clause to indicate the result or consequence of that extent.

💢 Application to the Given Question

To such an extent the multinational conglomerate has expanded...

In this sentence, the restrictive phrase "To such an extent" is placed at the beginning. Therefore, the subject "the multinational conglomerate" cannot be followed by the auxiliary verb "has". To correct the sentence, the auxiliary verb "has" must be moved to the position immediately preceding the subject.

Corrected Sentence

To such an extent has the multinational conglomerate expanded its operations into the emerging markets of Southeast Asia that it now controls nearly forty percent of the regional market share.

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 ✅: To such a degree did the noise increase that we could not hear each other speak.

Example 2 ✅: To such an extent has the pollution risen that the government has issued a health advisory.

Example 3 ✅: To such a degree was he involved in the scandal that he had to resign immediately.

questions.q_en:
Select the passive form of the following sentence.

"Let the recovery agents handle the hostile defaulter."
questions.q_hi:
Select the passive form of the following sentence.

"Let the recovery agents handle the hostile defaulter."
options_en: Let the hostile defaulter be handled by the recovery agents.
The hostile defaulter should be handled by the recovery agen
Let the hostile defaulter be handle by the recovery agents.
You are suggested to let the hostile defaulter handled.
options_hi: Let the hostile defaulter be handled by the recovery agents.
The hostile defaulter should be handled by the recovery agen
Let the hostile defaulter be handle by the recovery agents.
You are suggested to let the hostile defaulter handled.
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (A)

📌 Rule / Concept: Imperative with “Let” – Passive Formation
When an imperative sentence begins with “Let + object + base verb,” the passive structure becomes: Let + object + be + V³ (+ by + Subject). The word “be” is mandatory before the past participle. The base verb must change to its V³ form.

📌 Application to the Given Question

Let the recovery agents handle the hostile defaulter. Here, the structure is “Let + subject + base verb.” In passive voice, “the hostile defaulter” becomes the focus, and the correct structure is: Let + the hostile defaulter + be + handled + by the recovery agents. Option (B) changes the meaning to a suggestion using “should.” Option (C) is grammatically incorrect because it uses the base verb instead of V³ (“handle” instead of “handled”). Option (D) is structurally incorrect.

💡 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

For “Let + object + V¹,” use “Let + object + be + V³” in passive. Do not omit “be.” Always use the past participle (V³). Avoid changing the sentence into a different modal structure unless required.

questions.q_en:
In the following question, a sentence has been given in Direct/Indirect speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect/Direct speech.

The mentor said that it was time they started the project.
questions.q_hi:
In the following question, a sentence has been given in Direct/Indirect speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect/Direct speech.

The mentor said that it was time they started the project.
options_en: The mentor said, "It is time they started the project."
The mentor said, "It is time we start the project."
The mentor said, "It is time we started the project."
The mentor said, "It was time we started the project."
options_hi: The mentor said, "It is time they started the project."
The mentor said, "It is time we start the project."
The mentor said, "It is time we started the project."
The mentor said, "It was time we started the project."
questions.solution_en:
The correct answer is Option C: The mentor said, "It is time we started the project."

Key Points

  • The "It is time" Structure: In direct speech, the phrase "It is time" is always followed by the Simple Past (started) to show urgency. When converting back from "it was time," we must restore the original present tense "is" in the direct speech.

  • Pronoun Reversion: In the indirect speech, the pronoun is "they." Since the mentor is likely part of the group or addressing them directly, the original word in direct speech would be "we".

  • Tense Consistency:

    • Even though "started" is past tense, it is used in the Present Direct Speech because of the specific "It is time" rule.

    • Option B is a common trap because it uses the present tense "start." However, the rule explicitly requires the Past Form (started) even in the present tense direct speech.

  • Present Participle (V{ing}): Used when the noun performs the action.

  • Past Participle (V3): Used when the noun receives the action or is in a particular state because of the action.

"...only vaccinating employees are allowed to enter..."

  • If we say "vaccinated employees," it means the employees have received the vaccine themselves.

Since the safety regulation is about who is protected against the virus to enter a building, we need the passive form. The employees received the vaccine; therefore, they are vaccinated.

📌 Rule / Concept: Present Perfect with Ordinal Phrase

When a sentence uses an introductory phrase like "This is the first/second/third time...", "This is the best/worst...", or "This is the only...", it implies that an experience started in the past and is being completed or counted at the present moment. Therefore, the following clause must be in the Present Perfect Tense

💢 Application to the Given Question

"...this is the third time this month that the server... crashed unexpectedly..."

The sentence starts with "This is the third time," which acts as a counter for a recurring event within a period that includes the present (this month). To show the connection between the past occurrences and the current statement, the verb must be in the Present Perfect.

  • Incorrect: ...the third time the server crashed (Simple Past suggests the month is over).

  • Correct: ...the third time the server has crashed (Connects the event to the current "third" instance).

Corrected Sentence

This is the third time this month that the server of our main branch has crashed unexpectedly, resulting in a significant loss of productivity for the technical department.

questions.q_en:
When Arvind accepted the managerial position at a declining textile firm, he was aware that the challenge extended far beyond falling profits. The company’s real ailment lay buried in its culture—an unspoken resistance to accountability that had slowly normalized mediocrity. Employees met deadlines just well enough to avoid reprimand, innovation was quietly discouraged under the guise of “practicality,” and senior leadership equated stability with stagnation. Arvind initially chose restraint over disruption, believing that trust must precede transformation. However, this cautious approach was soon misinterpreted as indecision, reinforcing the very complacency he intended to dismantle.

As months passed, subtle patterns emerged. Suggestions were applauded in meetings but ignored in execution, data was selectively presented to justify inaction, and failures were attributed to external forces rather than internal inefficiencies. Arvind realized that the organization did not lack talent; it lacked the discomfort necessary for growth. When he finally introduced performance-linked evaluations and transparent reporting mechanisms, resistance intensified. Critics accused him of eroding harmony and imposing corporate rigidity on a “family-like” workplace. Yet beneath these objections lay a deeper fear—the loss of anonymity in collective failure. The turning point came not through dramatic reform but through consistency. Arvind refused to reverse decisions despite mounting pressure, yet he also resisted authoritarian impulses. Over time, clarity replaced confusion. While some employees exited, others adapted, discovering that accountability, though unsettling, offered professional dignity. The firm did not transform overnight, nor did it achieve spectacular success. But it shed its illusion of comfort, replacing it with a fragile yet honest culture—one where progress was measured not by immediate results, but by the willingness to confront inconvenient truths.

📌 Rule / Concept: Transitive Stative Verbs – Passive Formation
Even stative verbs like contain, hold, possess can form passive voice if they take a direct object. The standard passive structure in the simple present tense is: Object + is/am/are + V³. However, the preposition used in passive must be idiomatically correct. In the case of “contain,” the natural passive expression uses “contained in” rather than “contained by.”

📌 Application to the Given Question

This corporate locker contains the original title deeds of the property. Here, “contains” is a transitive verb with “the original title deeds of the property” as its object. Since the object exists, passive conversion is possible. The correct passive form is: “The original title deeds of the property are contained in this corporate locker.” Option (A) is grammatically awkward because “contained by” is not idiomatic in this context. Option (C) unnecessarily changes the tense to present perfect. Option (D) is incorrect because transitive stative verbs can form passive constructions.

💡 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

Stative verbs can form passive if they take a direct object. Maintain the original tense during conversion. Use natural prepositions in passive constructions. Avoid tense shifts unless required.

Rule/Concept: Possessive Case before a Gerund -

In formal English, when an -ing form of a verb (Gerund) functions as a noun, the noun or pronoun preceding it should be in the possessive case. This is because the emphasis is not on the person, but on the action the person is performing.

Key Rule:

Object Pronouns (Incorrect): me, him, her, us, them, you. ❌

Possessive Adjectives (Correct): my, his, her, our, their, your ✅

Application to the Given Question - ...depends on them finishing the technical documentation...

In this sentence, the object of the preposition "on" is the entire act of finishing (the gerund). The sentence isn't saying the project depends on them (the people); it depends on the finishing of the work. Therefore, we must use the possessive pronoun "their" to modify the gerund "finishing."

Corrected Sentence - The success of the project depends on their finishing the technical documentation on time to avoid any further delays in the manufacturing process.

More Examples for Clarity –

1. I was annoyed by his arriving late to the meeting. (Not: him arriving)

2. Do you mind my sitting here? (Not: me sitting)

questions.q_en: Their policy is that if you __________ not respect their deadlines, the manuscript will be automatically rejected.
questions.q_hi: Their policy is that if you __________ not respect their deadlines, the manuscript will be automatically rejected.
options_en:
Do

Will

did

would
options_hi:
Do

Will

did

would
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is – Option (A)

👉 Replace “___” with “do”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Conditional Sentences – First Conditional

The First Conditional is used to talk about real, possible, and likely future situations and their results.

Its standard structure is:

If + Present Simple, will + base form of verb

Key points:

 

  • The if-clause always takes Present Simple, not future tense.
  • Helping verbs like do / does are used in negative forms in the present simple.
  • Using will or would directly after if is grammatically incorrect in standard exam English (unless expressing willingness, which is rare and context-specific).

💢 Application to the Given Question

“…if you ___ not respect their deadlines…”

Here, the sentence states a real policy-based consequence that will occur in the future if a condition is not fulfilled.
Since the condition is real and possible, the First Conditional must be used.

 

  • Subject = you
  • Present simple negative form = do not respect

Using any future auxiliary (like will not) in the if-clause would violate the First Conditional rule.

✅ Corrected Sentence

Their policy is that if you do not respect their deadlines, the manuscript will be automatically rejected.
